mn36:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood.
mn36:2.1: Now on that occasion, it being morning, the Blessed One had finished dressing and had taken his bowl and (outer) robe, being desirous of going into Vesālī for alms.
mn36:3.1: Then as Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was walking and wandering for exercise he came to the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
mn36:3.2: The venerable Ānanda saw him coming in the distance.
mn36:3.3: When he saw him, he said to the Blessed One:
mn36:3.4: ‘Venerable sir, here comes Saccaka the Nigantha’s son; he is a debater, a clever speaker, and regarded by many as a saint.
mn36:3.5: He wants to decry the Enlightened One, to decry the Dhamma, to decry the Sangha.
mn36:3.6: It would be good if the Blessed One would sit down for a while out of compassion.’
mn36:3.7: The Blessed One sat down on the seat made ready.
mn36:3.8: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went up to him and exchanged greetings with him, and after the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:
mn36:4.1: ‘Master Gotama, there are some monks and divines who abide in pursuit of the practice of developing the body without developing the mind.
mn36:4.2: They are touched by bodily painful feeling.
mn36:4.3: It has happened that a man who is touched by bodily painful feeling got a paralysis of the thigh or his heart burst or hot blood gushed from his mouth or he went mad, out of his mind.
mn36:4.4: So then the mind was subservient to the body, it let the body wield mastery.
mn36:4.6: Because the mind was not developed.
mn36:4.7: But there are some monks and divines who abide in pursuit of developing the mind, without developing the body.
mn36:4.8: They are touched by mental painful feeling.
mn36:4.9: It has happened that a man touched by mental painful feeling also got a paralysis of the thigh or his heart burst or hot blood gushed from his mouth or he went mad, out of his mind.
mn36:4.10: So then the body was subservient to the mind, it let the mind wield mastery.
mn36:4.12: Because the body was not developed.
mn36:4.13: Master Gotama, it has occurred to me:
mn36:4.14: surely Master Gotama’s disciples abide in pursuit of developing the mind, without developing the body?’
mn36:5.1: ‘But Aggivessana, how has development of body been learnt by you?’
mn36:5.3: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Sankicca, Makkhali Gosāla.
mn36:5.4: They go naked, rejecting conventions, licking their hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked, they do not accept anything brought, or anything specially made, or an invitation;
mn36:5.5: they receive nothing out of a pot, from out of a bowl, across a threshold, across a stick, across a pestle, from two eating together, from a woman with child, from a woman giving suck, from (where) a woman is lying with a man, from where food is advertized to be distributed, from where a dog is waiting, from where flies are buzzing; they accept no fish or meat, they drink no wine or spirits or fermented liquor.
mn36:5.6: They keep to one house, to one morsel; they keep to two houses, to two morsels; … they keep to seven houses, to seven morsels.
mn36:5.7: They live on one saucerful, on two saucerfuls … on seven saucerfuls, a day.
mn36:5.8: They take food once each day, once each two days … once each seven days; and so up to once each fortnight, they dwell devoted to such practice of taking food at stated intervals.’
mn36:6.1: ‘But do they always subsist like that, Aggivessana?’
mn36:6.3: sometimes they chew good hard food, eat good soft food, taste good relishes, drink good drinks.
mn36:6.4: With that they pick up strength, wax and get fat.’
mn36:6.5: ‘What they once abandoned, Aggivessana, they later gather together again. That is how there is amassing and dispersal of this body.
mn36:6.6: Now how has development of mind been learnt by you?’
mn36:6.7: When Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was asked by the Blessed One about development of mind, he was unable to answer.
mn36:7.1: Then the Blessed One told him:
mn36:7.2: ‘What you have just spoken of as development of body, Aggivessana, is not developing the body according to Dhamma in the Noble Discipline.
mn36:7.3: Since you do not know what development of body is, how should you know what developing the mind is?
mn36:7.4: Nevertheless, Aggivessana, listen how a man is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind, and how he is developed in body and developed in mind,
mn36:7.5: and heed well what I shall say.’
mn36:7.6: ‘Even so, sir,’ Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied.
mn36:8.1: ‘How is man undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind?
mn36:8.2: Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in an untaught ordinary man.
mn36:8.3: Touched by that pleasant feeling, he lusts after that pleasant feeling, and he keeps lusting after that pleasant feeling.
mn36:8.4: That pleasant feeling of his ceases.
mn36:8.5: With the cessation of the pleasant feeling painful feeling (later) arises.
mn36:8.6: Touched by that painful feeling he sorrows, grieves and laments, beating his breast, he weeps and becomes distraught.
mn36:8.7: When that pleasant feeling is arisen in him, it invades the mind and remains because the body is not developed. And when that painful feeling is arisen in him, it invades the mind and remains because the mind is not developed.
mn36:8.8: Anyone in whom, in this double manner, pleasant feeling arisen invades the mind and remains because the body is not developed, and painful feeling arisen invades the mind and remains because the mind is not developed, is thus undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
mn36:9.1: And how is man developed in body and developed in mind?
mn36:9.2: Here, Aggivessana, pleasant feeling arises in a well-taught noble disciple.
mn36:9.3: Touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not lust after that pleasant feeling, he does not keep lusting after that pleasant feeling.
mn36:9.4: That pleasant feeling of his ceases.
mn36:9.5: With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, painful feeling (later) arises.
mn36:9.6: Touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve or lament, he does not, beating his breast, weep and become distraught.
mn36:9.7: When that pleasant feeling is arisen in him it does not invade the mind and remain because the body is developed. And when that painful feeling is arisen in him, it does not invade the mind and remain because the mind is developed.
mn36:9.8: Anyone in whom, in this double manner, pleasant feeling arisen does not invade the mind and remain because the body is developed, and painful feeling arisen does not invade the mind and remain because the mind is developed, is thus developed in mind and developed in body.’
mn36:10.1: ‘I have confidence in Master Gotama thus:
mn36:10.2: “He is developed in body and developed in mind.”’
mn36:10.3: ‘Surely, Aggivessana, the words you have spoken are directly personal.
mn36:10.5: Since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, that pleasant feeling arisen might invade my mind and remain, or that painful feeling arisen might invade my mind and remain — that is not possible.’
mn36:11.1: ‘Has there perhaps never arisen in Master Gotama a feeling so pleasant as to invade his mind and remain? Has there perhaps never arisen in Master Gotama a feeling so painful as to invade his mind and remain?’
mn36:12.2: Here, before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta I thought:
mn36:12.3: “House life is a constraint and it is a place of dirt; life gone forth is wide open.
mn36:12.4: It is not possible while living in a house to lead the life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.
mn36:12.5: Suppose I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”
mn36:13.1: So, Aggivessana, at a later time, while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
mn36:13.2: Having thus gone forth in search of what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:
mn36:13.3: ‘Friend Kālāma, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and discipline.’
mn36:13.4: When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma said to me:
mn36:13.6: This Dhamma is such that a wise man can soon enter upon and abide in it, realizing for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’
mn36:13.7: I quickly learned that Dhamma, Aggivessana.
mn36:13.8: As far as mere lip-reciting and mere repeating was concerned, I could speak the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I could claim, ‘I know and see,’ as could others.
mn36:13.10: ‘It is not through mere faith alone that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “By realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this Dhamma”;
mn36:13.11: certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’
mn36:13.12: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:
mn36:13.13: ‘Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare that by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge you enter upon and abide in this Dhamma?’
mn36:13.14: When this was said, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the base of nothingness.
mn36:13.16: ‘Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has faith; I too have faith.
mn36:13.17: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has energy; I too have energy.
mn36:13.18: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.
mn36:13.19: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has concentration; I too have concentration.
mn36:13.20: Not only Āḷāra Kālāma has wisdom; I too have wisdom.
mn36:13.21: Suppose I endeavour to realize the Dhamma that Āḷāra Kālāma declares he enters upon and abides in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.’
mn36:13.22: I quickly entered upon and abided in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, Aggivessana.
mn36:14.1: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and said to him:
mn36:14.2: ‘Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare that by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge you enter upon and abide in this Dhamma?’
mn36:14.3: ‘That is how I declare it, friend.’
mn36:14.4: ‘I too, friend, in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge.’
mn36:14.5: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is very good for us,
mn36:14.6: that we see such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.
mn36:14.7: So the Dhamma I declare I have realized for myself with direct knowledge is the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge;
mn36:14.8: and the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge, is the Dhamma I declare I have realized for myself with direct knowledge.
mn36:14.9: So the Dhamma I know is the Dhamma you know, and the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma I know.
mn36:14.10: As I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.
mn36:14.11: Come, friend, let us now lead this group together.’
mn36:14.12: Thus, Aggivessana, Āḷāra Kālāma, my teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself and honoured me with high honour.
mn36:14.14: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only as far as the base of nothingness.’
mn36:14.15: So, being dissatisfied with that Dhamma, I left it and went away.
mn36:15.1: So, Aggivessana, still searching for what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:
mn36:15.2: ‘Friend, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and discipline.’
mn36:15.3: When this was said, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta said to me:
mn36:15.5: This Dhamma is such that a wise man can soon enter upon and abide in it, realizing for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.’
mn36:15.6: I quickly learned that Dhamma, Aggivessana.
mn36:15.7: As far as mere lip-reciting and mere repeating was concerned, I could speak the doctrine of knowledge and the doctrine of the elders, and I could claim, ‘I know and see,’ as could others.
mn36:15.9: ‘It was not through mere faith alone that Rāma declared: “By realizing it for myself with direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in this Dhamma”;
mn36:15.10: certainly Rāma abided knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’
mn36:15.11: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:
mn36:15.12: ‘Friend, in what way did Rāma declare that by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge he entered upon and abided in this Dhamma?’
mn36:15.13: When this was said, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn36:15.15: ‘Not only Rāma had faith; I too have faith.
mn36:15.16: Not only Rāma had energy; I too have energy.
mn36:15.17: Not only Rāma had mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.
mn36:15.18: Not only Rāma had concentration; I too have concentration.
mn36:15.19: Not only Rāma had wisdom; I too have wisdom.
mn36:15.20: Suppose I endeavour to realize the Dhamma that Rāma declared he entered upon and abided in by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.’
mn36:15.21: I quickly entered upon and abided in that Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, Aggivessana.
mn36:15.22: Then, Aggivessana, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and said to him:
mn36:15.23: ‘Friend, is it in this way that Rāma declared that by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge he entered upon and abided in this Dhamma?’
mn36:15.24: ‘That is how Rāma declared it, friend.’
mn36:15.25: ‘I too, friend, in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, having realized it for myself with direct knowledge.’
mn36:15.26: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is very good for us,
mn36:15.27: that we see such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.
mn36:15.28: So the Dhamma Rāma declared he had realized for himself with direct knowledge is the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge; and the Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, having realized it for yourself with direct knowledge, is the Dhamma Rāma declared he had realized for himself with direct knowledge.
mn36:15.29: So the Dhamma Rāma directly knew is the Dhamma you know, and the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma Rāma directly knew.
mn36:15.30: As Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
mn36:15.31: Come, friend, now you lead this group.’
mn36:15.32: Thus, Aggivessana, Uddaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the life divine, placed me in the position of teacher and honoured me with high honour.
mn36:15.34: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only as far as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’
mn36:15.35: So, being dissatisfied with that Dhamma, I left it and went away.
mn36:16.1: So, Aggivessana, still searching for what is good, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, walking by stages through the Magadhan country, I eventually arrived at Uruvelā, at Senānigama.
mn36:16.2: There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove, a clear-flowing river with pleasant, smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.
mn36:16.4: ‘This is an agreeable piece of ground, this delightful grove, this clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.
mn36:16.5: This will serve for the endeavour of a clansman who seeks endeavour.’
mn36:17.1: ‘Now these three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:17.2: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water,
mn36:17.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn36:17.4: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;
mn36:17.5: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn36:17.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying in water?’
mn36:17.9: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, and besides, it is lying in water.
mn36:17.10: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’
mn36:17.11: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives still bodily and mentally not withdrawn from sensual desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever for sensual desires are not quite abandoned and quieted within him, then, even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment,
mn36:17.12: and even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.
mn36:17.13: This was the first simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:18.1: Again, a second simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:18.2: Suppose there were a wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,
mn36:18.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn36:18.4: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;
mn36:18.5: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn36:18.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing with it the wet, sappy piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?’
mn36:18.9: Because it is a wet, sappy piece of wood, though it is lying on dry land far from water.
mn36:18.10: So the man would reap weariness and disappointment.’
mn36:18.11: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives still only bodily withdrawn from sensual desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever, for sensual desires are not quite abandoned and quieted within him, then even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment. And even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is incapable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.
mn36:18.12: This was the second simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:19.1: Again, a third simile occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:19.2: Suppose there were a dry sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water,
mn36:19.3: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn36:19.4: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;
mn36:19.5: how do you conceive this, Aggivessana,
mn36:19.6: would the man light a fire and produce heat by rubbing with it the dry, sapless piece of wood lying on dry land far from water?’
mn36:19.9: Because it is a dry, sapless piece of wood, and besides, it is lying on dry land far from water!’
mn36:19.10: ‘So, Aggivessana, while a monk or divine lives both bodily and mentally withdrawn from sense-desires, and while his lust, affection, passion, thirst and fever, for sensual desires are quite abandoned and quieted within him, then, even if the good monk or divine feels painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is capable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment, and even if the good monk or divine does not feel painful, racking, piercing feelings due to striving, he is capable of knowledge and vision and the supreme enlightenment.
mn36:19.11: This was the third simile that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:19.12: These, Aggivessana, were the three similes that occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.
mn36:20.2: “Suppose, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrain and crush mind with mind?”
mn36:20.3: So, with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained and crushed mind with mind.
mn36:20.4: While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits.
mn36:20.5: Just as a strong man might seize a weaker by the head or shoulders and beat him down, constrain and crush him,
mn36:20.6: so too, while with my teeth clenched and my tongue pressed against the roof of my mouth, I beat down, constrained and crushed mind with mind, sweat ran from my armpits.
mn36:20.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:20.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:21.2: “Suppose I practise the meditation without breathing?”
mn36:21.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth and nose.
mn36:21.4: While I did so, there was a loud sound of winds coming from my ear-holes.
mn36:21.5: Just as there is a loud sound when a smith’s bellows are blown,
mn36:21.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth and nose, there was a loud sound of winds coming from my ear-holes.
mn36:21.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:21.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:22.2: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”
mn36:22.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.
mn36:22.4: While I did so, violent winds harried my head.
mn36:22.5: Just as if a strong man were splitting my head open with a sharp sword,
mn36:22.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, violent winds harried my head.
mn36:22.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:22.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:23.2: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”
mn36:23.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.
mn36:23.4: While I did so, there were violent pains in my head.
mn36:23.5: Just as if a strong man were tightening a tough leather strap round my head as a headband,
mn36:23.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, there were violent pains in my head.
mn36:23.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:23.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:24.2: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”
mn36:24.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.
mn36:24.4: While I did so, violent winds carved up my belly.
mn36:24.5: Just as a clever butcher or his apprentice carves up an ox’s belly with a sharp knife,
mn36:24.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, violent winds carved up my belly.
mn36:24.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:24.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:25.2: “Suppose I practise further the meditation without breathing?”
mn36:25.3: So I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears.
mn36:25.4: While I did so, there was violent burning in my body.
mn36:25.5: Just as if two strong men had seized a weaker man by both arms and were roasting him over a pit of hot coals,
mn36:25.6: so too, while I stopped the in-breaths and out-breaths in my mouth, nose and ears, there was a violent burning in my body.
mn36:25.7: But although tireless energy was aroused in me and unremitting mindfulness was established, yet my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by the painful endeavour.
mn36:25.8: But such painful feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:26.1: ‘Now when gods saw me, they said:
mn36:26.4: “The monk Gotama is not dead, he is dying.”
mn36:26.6: “The monk Gotama is neither dead nor dying; he is an Arahant, for such is the way of Arahants.”
mn36:27.3: Then gods came to me and said:
mn36:27.4: “Good sir, do not entirely cut off food.
mn36:27.5: If you do so, we shall inject heavenly food into your pores and you will live on that.”
mn36:27.7: “If I claim to be completely fasting and these gods inject heavenly food into my pores and I live on that, then I shall be lying.”
mn36:27.8: I dismissed those gods, saying: “There is no need.”’
mn36:28.2: “Suppose I take very little food, say, a handful each time, whether it is bean soup or lentil soup or vetch soup or pea soup?”
mn36:28.3: So I took very little food, a handful each time, whether it was bean soup or lentil soup or vetch soup or pea soup.
mn36:28.4: While I did so, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation.
mn36:28.5: Because of eating so little my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems.
mn36:28.6: Because of eating so little my backside became like a camel’s hoof.
mn36:28.7: Because of eating so little the projections on my spine stood forth like corded beads.
mn36:28.8: Because of eating so little my ribs jutted out as gaunt as the crazy rafters of an old roofless barn.
mn36:28.9: Because of eating so little the gleam of my eyes sunk far down in their sockets looked like the gleam of water sunk far down in a deep well.
mn36:28.10: Because of eating so little my scalp shrivelled and withered as a green gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun.
mn36:28.11: Because of eating so little, if I touched my belly skin, I encountered my backbone too; if I touched my backbone I encountered my belly skin too.
mn36:28.12: Because of eating so little, if I tried to make water or evacuate my bowels, I fell over on my face there.
mn36:28.13: Because of eating so little, if I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body as I rubbed.
mn36:29.1: ‘Now when human beings saw me, they said: “The monk Gotama is a black man.”
mn36:29.2: Other human beings said: “The monk Gotama is not a black man, he is a brown man.”
mn36:29.3: Other human beings said: “The monk Gotama is neither a black nor a brown man, he is a fair-skinned man.”
mn36:29.4: So much had the clear, bright colour of my skin deteriorated through eating so little.
mn36:30.2: “Whenever a monk or divine in the past has felt painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.
mn36:30.3: And whenever a monk or divine in the future will feel painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.
mn36:30.4: And whenever a monk or divine at present feels painful, racking, piercing feeling due to striving, it can equal this but not exceed it.
mn36:30.5: But by this gruelling penance I have attained no distinction higher than the human state worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision.
mn36:30.6: Might there be another way to enlightenment?”
mn36:31.2: “I recall that, while my Sakyan father was busy, while I was sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn36:31.3: Might that be the way to enlightenment?”
mn36:31.4: Then, following on that memory, came the recognition:
mn36:32.2: “Why am I afraid of that pleasure? It is pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual desires and unprofitable dhammas.”
mn36:32.4: “I am not afraid of that pleasure, since it has nothing to do with sensual desires and unprofitable dhammas.”
mn36:33.2: “It is not possible to attain that pleasure with a body so excessively emaciated. Suppose I ate some solid food—some boiled rice and bread?”
mn36:33.3: And I ate some solid food—some boiled rice and bread.
mn36:33.4: But at that time five bhikkhus were waiting upon me, thinking:
mn36:33.5: “If the monk Gotama achieves something he will tell us.”
mn36:33.6: As soon as I ate the boiled rice and bread the five bhikkhus were disgusted and left me, thinking:
mn36:33.7: “The monk Gotama has turned self-indulgent, he has given up the endeavour and reverted to luxury.”
mn36:34.1: ‘Now when I had eaten solid food and regained strength, then quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, I entered upon and abode in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn36:34.2: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:35-37.1: With the stilling of initial and sustained application, I entered upon and abode in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and singleness of mind without initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.
mn36:35-37.2: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:35-37.3: With the fading away as well of happiness, I abided in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, I still felt pleasure with the body; I entered upon and abode in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’
mn36:35-37.4: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:35-37.5: With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered upon and abode in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn36:35-37.6: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:38.1: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past life.
mn36:38.2: I recollected my manifold past life, that is, one birth, two births … thus with details and particulars I recollected my manifold past life.
mn36:39.1: This was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;
mn36:39.2: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.
mn36:39.3: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:40.1: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing-away and reappearance of beings.
mn36:40.2: With the heavenly eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions …
mn36:41.1: This was the second true knowledge attained by me in the second watch of the night;
mn36:41.2: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.
mn36:41.3: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:42.1: ‘When my concentrated mind was thus purified, clear, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and had become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.
mn36:42.2: I directly knew as it actually is: “This is suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the origin of suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
mn36:42.3: I directly knew as it actually is: “These are the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the origin of the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the cessation of the taints”; I directly knew as it actually is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.”
mn36:43.1: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance.
mn36:43.2: When it was liberated there came the knowledge: “It is liberated.”
mn36:43.3: I directly knew: “Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this to come.”’
mn36:44.1: This was the third true knowledge attained by me in the third watch of the night;
mn36:44.2: ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent and self-controlled.
mn36:44.3: But such pleasant feeling as arose in me did not invade my mind and remain.
mn36:45.1: ‘I have direct knowledge of preaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds, Aggivessana.
mn36:45.2: Perhaps someone or other has imagined:
mn36:45.3: “The monk Gotama is preaching the Dhamma at me.”
mn36:45.4: But it should not be regarded so:
mn36:45.5: a Tathāgata preaches the Dhamma to others only to give them knowledge.
mn36:45.6: When the talk is finished, Aggivessana, then I settle my mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness and concentrate it on that same sign for concentration as before, in which I constantly abide.’
mn36:45.7: ‘That is believable (as a statement) of Master Gotama’s since he is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn36:45.8: But perhaps Master Gotama has also had direct knowledge of sleeping by day?’
mn36:46.1: ‘In the last month of the hot season, Aggivessana, on return from the alms-round after the meal, I have had direct knowledge of laying out my cloak of patches folded in four, and lying down on the right side and falling asleep, mindful and fully aware.’
mn36:46.2: ‘Some monks and divines call that a deluded man’s abiding, Master Gotama.’
mn36:46.3: ‘That is not how a man is deluded or not deluded, Aggivessana.
mn36:46.4: Listen rather how a man is deluded or not deluded,
mn36:46.5: and heed well what I shall say.’
mn36:46.6: ‘Even so, sir,’ Saccaka the Nigantha’s son replied.
mn36:47.1: ‘Him I call deluded, Aggivessana, in whom taints that defile, produce renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death are unabandoned;
mn36:47.2: for it is with the non-abandoning of taints that a man is deluded.
mn36:47.3: Him I call undeluded in whom such taints as defile, as produce renewal of being, as give trouble, as ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned;
mn36:47.4: for it is with the abandoning of taints that a man is undeluded.
mn36:47.5: In a Tathāgata, such taints as produce renewal of being, as give trouble, as ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that their nature to arise in the future is no more.
mn36:47.6: Just as a palm tree with its top cut off is incapable of growing,
mn36:47.7: so too, in a Tathāgata the taints that defile, produce renewal of being, give trouble, ripen in suffering, and lead to future birth, ageing and death, are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that their nature to arise in future is no more.’
mn36:48.1: When this was said, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son said:
mn36:48.2: ‘It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvellous,
mn36:48.3: how, when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened!
mn36:48.4: I have had direct knowledge of engaging Purāṇa Kassapa in argument,
mn36:48.5: and then he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate and surliness.
mn36:48.6: But when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn36:48.7: I have had direct knowledge of engaging Makkhali Gosāla …
mn36:48.12: and then he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and showed anger, hate and surliness.
mn36:48.13: But when Master Gotama has personal remarks directed at him again and again thus, the colour of his skin brightens and the colour of his face clears, as is to be expected in one who is Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn36:48.14: And now, Master Gotama, we depart;
mn36:48.15: we are busy and have much to do.’
mn36:48.16: ‘It is time now to do as you think fit, Aggivessana.’
mn36:48.17: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son was satisfied, and delighting in the Blessed One’s words, he got up from his seat and departed.
